transcript.en: Every year my second-year students can recite the formula for a confidence interval. Then I ask what the ninety five percent refers to, and most say: the chance the true mean is inside this interval. Today: where a standard error comes from, how the bootstrap estimates it, and how to teach both without hand-waving. An estimate, such as a sample mean, is a random variable. Its sampling distribution is the spread of values it would take over all possible samples of the same size from the same population. The standard deviation of that distribution is the standard error. For a mean it is sigma over the square root of n, so four times the data only halves the error. The central limit theorem says the shape is close to normal for large n. We drew a thousand samples of thirty exam marks from a skewed population and plotted the means. The marks were skewed, but the means pile up in a near-normal hill around the true mean. In real research we have one sample, not a thousand. Efron's bootstrap resamples that one sample with replacement, recomputes the estimate many times, and uses the spread of those values as the standard error. Students meet the formula first and the idea never. Reverse that. Let them simulate many samples before any algebra, then derive sigma over root n to explain what they already saw. Quick check! A ninety five percent confidence interval for a mean is from sixty to sixty eight. Which statement is correct? The ninety five percent describes the method, not this one interval. Over many samples, about ninety five in a hundred intervals built this way would contain the true mean. In the app, open the sampling lab. Draw hundreds of samples, change the sample size, and watch the spread of the means shrink like one over root n. Your turn. A study has a standard error of four. How many times more data do we need to bring it down to two? Four times as much data. Remember: an estimate has a sampling distribution, its spread is the standard error, and the bootstrap estimates it from one sample. Try it in your next lecture: before showing any formula, give pairs a dataset and ask them to resample it two hundred times and plot the means. Then ask them to predict what happens when n is four times larger.

title.en: Where a standard error comes from

body.en:
An estimator is a function of random data, so it is itself a random variable. Its sampling distribution is the distribution of its values over repeated samples of size n from the same population; the standard deviation of that distribution is the standard error. For the sample mean, SE = σ/√n, and the central limit theorem gives an approximately normal shape for large n whatever the population’s shape (Wasserman, 2004).

In practice we see one sample. Efron’s (1979) bootstrap treats that sample as a stand-in for the population: draw B resamples of size n with replacement, recompute the statistic on each, and use their standard deviation as the SE, or their 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as a percentile interval. It works for medians, correlations and model coefficients where no tidy formula exists, but it cannot repair a biased sample, and it is unreliable for extremes such as the maximum.

The research on teaching is consistent: students who meet the formula first tend to read a 95% interval as a 95% chance that this interval holds μ. Simulation-first sequences, as recommended in the GAISE College Report (2016), let students see the long-run behaviour of the procedure before any algebra, and then the formula explains what they have already observed.

transcript.en: A student brought me a project with ninety nine percent accuracy. I asked one question: accuracy on what? It was the same data the model was trained on. On new data, it fell to sixty one. Today: the bias–variance trade-off, honest error estimates with cross-validation, and the leakage mistakes students make. For squared error, the expected error on a new point splits into three parts: bias squared, variance, and noise we can never remove. Simple models have high bias. Flexible models have high variance. As complexity grows, training error keeps falling, but test error falls and then rises again. The best model sits at the bottom of that U, not at the lowest training error. We fitted polynomials of degree one to fifteen to two hundred points. Test error was lowest at degree four. By degree fifteen the curve wiggled through every training point and missed new ones. Cross-validation estimates test error without wasting data. Split the data into k folds, train on k minus one, test on the one left out, and average over all k. Five or ten folds is the usual choice. The commonest student bug is leakage. They scale or select features on all the data, then split. The test fold has already shaped the model. Every preprocessing step must be fitted inside each training fold. Quick check! Model A has training error two and test error twenty. Model B has training error twelve and test error fourteen. Which should we choose, and why? Model B. The gap in model A between two and twenty is the signature of high variance. We judge models on data they have not seen. In the app, open the overfitting lab. Raise the model's complexity step by step and watch training error fall while test error turns back up. Your turn. A student standardises all the data, then runs five-fold cross-validation. Is the estimate honest? No, it leaks. Remember: error is bias plus variance plus noise, choose the bottom of the U, and fit every step inside the training fold. Try it in your next lecture: hand out two short notebooks, one with leakage and one without. Then ask pairs to find why their cross-validation scores differ before you explain.

body.en:
For squared-error loss, the expected error at a new point decomposes as bias² + variance + irreducible noise (Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, 2009). Rigid models miss real structure (high bias); flexible models chase noise in the particular sample (high variance). Training error falls monotonically with flexibility, while test error traces a U, so the training score is not evidence of predictive skill.

k-fold cross-validation estimates test error by rotating a held-out fold: train on k − 1 folds, score the remaining one, and average. Five or ten folds trade bias against the variance of the estimate well (James et al., ISLR). Use it to choose a model or tuning parameter, then report performance on a final test set that was never used for any choice; otherwise the reported score is optimistic.

The classroom failure is leakage: scaling, imputing or selecting features on the full data before splitting, or splitting rows of the same patient or student across folds. Teach preprocessing as part of the model, fitted inside each training fold, for example with a scikit-learn Pipeline, and make students state their unit of independence before they split.

transcript.en: Our faculty found that students who used the tutoring centre had lower grades. A dean proposed closing it. Before anyone voted, I asked: who chooses to go to tutoring? Today: why correlation misleads, how a causal diagram tells you what to adjust for, and how difference-in-differences estimates an effect. A confounder causes both the treatment and the outcome. Here, prior struggle sends students to tutoring and also lowers grades. The raw comparison mixes the effect of tutoring with the effect of struggling. Pearl's causal diagrams make assumptions explicit. Arrows mean direct causes. To estimate an effect, block every back-door path by adjusting for confounders. But never adjust for a collider or a mediator. One department added tutoring in a new term; another did not. The first rose from sixty to seventy. The second rose from sixty two to sixty six anyway. Some of that rise would have happened without tutoring. Difference-in-differences subtracts the comparison group's change from the treated group's change. Ten minus four gives an effect of six points. It assumes both groups would have moved in parallel without the treatment. Students learn causal reasoning best when they must defend a decision. Give them a real policy question, ask them to draw the diagram first, and grade the assumptions they state, not only the number. Quick check! Tutoring affects study hours, and study hours affect grades. To estimate the total effect of tutoring on grades, should we adjust for study hours? No. Study hours are a mediator, part of how tutoring works. Adjusting for them removes some of the very effect we want to measure. In the app, open the scatter lab. Plot grade against tutoring hours, then colour points by prior grade and see how the trend changes within each group. Your turn. Treated group: from fifty to fifty eight. Comparison group: from fifty two to fifty five. What is the difference-in-differences estimate? Five points: eight minus three. Remember: draw the diagram, adjust for confounders but not mediators, and use a comparison group with parallel trends. body.en:
A causal effect compares what happens to the same units with and without a treatment, one of which we never observe. Randomisation solves this by making groups comparable on average. Without it, a confounder that drives both treatment and outcome biases the raw comparison, and in extreme cases reverses it, as in Simpson’s paradox.

Pearl’s (2009) directed acyclic graphs make the assumptions explicit. The back-door criterion says: to estimate the effect of X on Y, adjust for a set of variables that blocks every back-door path from X to Y and contains no descendant of X. So adjust for confounders, but not for mediators (they carry the effect) or colliders (conditioning on them opens a spurious path).

With panel data, difference-in-differences subtracts the comparison group’s change from the treated group’s change, removing fixed group differences and common shocks (Angrist and Pischke, 2009). Its key assumption, parallel trends, cannot be proved, but pre-period trends can be inspected. In teaching, grade the stated diagram and assumptions as heavily as the estimate: that is where causal reasoning lives.

يقارن الأثر السببي ما يحدث للوحدات نفسها مع المعالجة ودونها، وإحدى الحالتين لا نراها أبدًا. ويحلّ التوزيع العشوائي ذلك بجعل المجموعات متكافئة في المتوسط. ومن دونه، يحيّز المتغير المربك الذي يؤثر في المعالجة والنتيجة معًا المقارنة الخام، وقد يعكسها في الحالات القصوى، كما في مفارقة سيمبسون.

وتجعل المخططات اللادورية الموجّهة عند بيرل (٢٠٠٩) الافتراضات صريحة. ويقول معيار الباب الخلفي: لتقدير أثر X في Y، عدّل على مجموعة متغيرات تحجب كل مسار خلفي من X إلى Y ولا تحوي أي متغير ناتج عن X. فعدّل على المربكات، لا على الوسطاء (فهي تحمل الأثر) ولا على متغيرات التصادم (فالتكييف عليها يفتح مسارًا زائفًا).

transcript.en: My final exam was all calculations. My best students got top marks, then in their first internship they could not decide which analysis a real question needed. I had taught the tools, not the judgement. Today: how to align a statistics or data-science module, design real projects, require reproducible work, and grade it fairly with a rubric. Biggs calls it constructive alignment. Write the learning outcomes first, using verbs like analyse and justify. Then choose activities that practise those verbs, and assessments that measure them. The GAISE college report asks for real data and real questions. A good project starts from a question the student cares about, uses messy public data, and ends with a claim, its uncertainty, and its limits. Here is one way to spend fourteen weeks: four on inference, four on modelling, two on causal questions, and four on a staged project with a proposal, a draft and a final report. Require every submission to run from raw data to final figure with one command, in a notebook or script under version control. If a marker cannot rerun it, it is not finished. This also discourages copied results. Share the rubric when you set the project, not when you grade it. Describe each level in words a student can act on, and give feedback on the draft. Hattie and Timperley show feedback works when it says where to go next. Quick check! An outcome says students will justify the choice of a statistical model. The only assessment is a timed multiple choice test of formulas. Is this aligned? No. Justify is the verb, and a formula test cannot see a justification. A short written defence of a model choice on real data would measure it. In the app, open the histogram lab. Change the bin width on the same data and notice how the story changes. Use it to show students why every choice in an analysis must be justified. Your turn. When should students first see the project rubric? When the project is set. Remember: align outcomes, activities and assessment, use real projects, require reproducible work, and share the rubric early. Try it this week: take your module's learning outcomes, underline each verb, and next to it write the assessment that measures it. Any verb with nothing beside it needs a new task.

title.en: Teach the judgement, not just the tools

body.en:
Biggs and Tang’s constructive alignment starts from intended learning outcomes written with active verbs (analyse, justify, critique), then chooses teaching activities that practise those verbs and assessments that measure them. In data science the gap is usually between outcomes about judgement and exams about calculation; Anderson and Krathwohl’s revised taxonomy helps you check which level each task really reaches.

The GAISE College Report (2016) recommends teaching statistical thinking with real data, using technology, and fostering active learning; Freeman et al.'s (2014) meta-analysis found active learning cut failure rates in STEM courses substantially compared with lecturing alone. A staged project, with a proposal, a draft and a final report, gives students the iterative practice the field needs and gives you points to intervene.

Make reproducibility a requirement, not a bonus: one command from raw data to every figure, under version control. Share a rubric when you set the project, describe each level in actionable terms, and give feedback on drafts that answers Hattie and Timperley’s (2007) three questions: where am I going, how am I going, and where to next?
body.ar:
يبدأ التنسيق البنّاء عند Biggs وTang من نواتج تعلّم مقصودة مكتوبة بأفعال نشطة (يحلّل، يبرّر، ينقد)، ثم يختار أنشطة تدريس تمارس تلك الأفعال وتقييمات تقيسها. وفي علم البيانات تقع الفجوة عادة بين نواتج تتعلق بالحكم وامتحانات تتعلق بالحساب، ويساعدك تصنيف Anderson وKrathwohl المنقّح على التحقق من المستوى الذي تبلغه كل مهمة فعلًا.

ويوصي تقرير GAISE الجامعي (٢٠١٦) بتدريس التفكير الإحصائي ببيانات حقيقية، واستخدام التقنية، وتشجيع التعلّم النشط، ووجد التحليل البعدي لـ Freeman وآخرين (٢٠١٤) أن التعلّم النشط خفّض نسب الرسوب في مقررات العلوم والتقنية بدرجة كبيرة مقارنة بالمحاضرة وحدها. ويمنح المشروع المرحلي، بمقترح ومسودة وتقرير نهائي، الطلاب الممارسة التكرارية التي يحتاجها المجال، ويمنحك نقاطًا للتدخل.

واجعل قابلية التكرار شرطًا لا مكافأة: أمر واحد من البيانات الخام إلى كل رسم، تحت التحكم في النسخ. وشارك معيار التقييم عند التكليف بالمشروع، وصِف كل مستوى بعبارات قابلة للتنفيذ، وقدّم ملاحظات على المسودات تجيب عن أسئلة Hattie وTimperley (٢٠٠٧) الثلاثة: إلى أين أذهب، وكيف أتقدّم، وما الخطوة التالية؟
